Start here

The solving framework

Location → lineage/morphology → spread behavior → marker/mutation → paraneoplastic clue → treatment implication.

Fast first split: Is this small cell or non-small cell? The lecture makes this the highest-value early distinction because it changes treatment strategy.
  1. Where is it? Central airway-based favors squamous or small cell; peripheral/pleural-based favors adenocarcinoma.
  2. What does it look like? Keratin pearls, glands, small round blue cells, neuroendocrine nests, or pleural spindle/epithelioid tumor.
  3. What marker confirms lineage? p40, TTF-1/napsin, synaptophysin/chromogranin, or calretinin.
  4. What clue changes the question? EGFR/KRAS, ADH/ACTH/PTHrP, apical invasion, carcinoid criteria, or asbestos.

Exam sheet

Part I — Core framework & must-know content

Core map: risk/exposure → site & cell of origin → morphology → marker → molecular behavior → local/metastatic consequence → treatment logic.

1. Staging, spread, and treatment logic

Lecture conceptExam-ready rule
T size binsT1a ≤1 cm; T1b 1–2 cm; T1c 2–3 cm; T2 3–5 cm; T3 5–7 cm; T4 >7 cm or major invasion/ipsilateral nodule per the lecture slide.
Nodal progressionN1 = local hilar/intrapulmonary; more advanced mediastinal/contralateral/supraclavicular nodal disease raises stage and systemic-spread risk.
Stage implicationNo nodal spread / localized early tumor → surgery can be curative. Nodal or locally advanced disease → multimodal/systemic treatment becomes more important. Distant disease → systemic strategy dominates.
Metastatic sites emphasizedAdrenal 50%, liver 30–50%, brain 20%, bone 20% on the slide.
Malignant pleural effusionPlaced in the metastatic M1 / stage IV discussion by the lecturer.

2. Risk factors & presentation

Risk clueLecture emphasis
SmokingDominant risk; both duration and intensity matter. Slide: 80% of lung cancers occur in active smokers.
Secondhand smokeRisk is increased vs nonsmokers.
RadonColorless/odorless/tasteless radioactive gas from uranium/thorium/radium decay; can seep into buildings.
OtherAsbestos, uranium mining, radiation exposure, family history, certain beta-carotene supplementation in smokers.
Never-smokerThink adenocarcinoma, often women, with EGFR emphasized.
Presentation clueWhy
Cough / dyspneaCentral airway involvement/obstruction.
HemoptysisTumor bleeding into airway.
Post-obstructive pneumoniaAirway blockage → secretion stasis/infection.
Weight lossSystemic malignancy effect.
Chest/back/shoulder painExtension into pleura, mediastinum, chest wall, nerves.

3. Tumor master table

TumorLocation / morphologyMarkers / molecularHigh-value associations
SquamousCentral, bronchus-centered, cauliflower-like, necrotic gray-white; keratin pearls if differentiated.p40+, CK5/6+, TTF-1−. CDKN2A/p16, TP53, RB loss; FGFR1 amplification.Smoking/metaplasia sequence; PTHrP → hypercalcemia.
AdenocarcinomaPeripheral/pleural-based, pleural puckering; gland-forming; lepidic/acinar/papillary/solid/micropapillary patterns.TTF-1+, napsin+. EGFR/ALK/ROS/MET/RET; KRAS in smokers; EGFR emphasized in never-smokers.Most common type in the lecture classification; never-smoker association.
Small cellCentral; small round blue cells, scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, salt-and-pepper chromatin, extensive necrosis.Synaptophysin/chromogranin/INSM1; Ki-67 >90%; TP53 + RB loss; MYC amplification.Very aggressive, early nodal/metastatic spread; chemo/radiation focus; ADH/ACTH; Lambert-Eaton listed.
Large cellLarge malignant cells without defining squamous/adeno/small-cell morphology.No defining lineage IHC in the lecture.Diagnosis of exclusion.
CarcinoidUsually endobronchial; nests/sheets/trabeculae, salt-and-pepper chromatin; can cause bronchiectasis/atelectasis from obstruction.Synaptophysin/chromogranin; dense-core granules.Typical vs atypical by mitoses/necrosis; usually younger patients.
MesotheliomaDiffuse pleural tumor that encases lung; epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or mixed.Calretinin+.Asbestos; ferruginous bodies; pleural origin.

Invaded structureFinding
Recurrent laryngeal nerveHoarseness
Stellate ganglion / sympathetic chainHorner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis
Superior vena cavaFacial/upper-extremity edema, venous distention, plethora, dyspnea/headache
Brachial plexusShoulder pain + sensorimotor deficits / intrinsic-hand-muscle atrophy
Phrenic nerveHemidiaphragm paralysis

5. Molecular logic

Acceleration problem — adenocarcinoma: gain-of-function signaling in tyrosine-kinase pathways → growth signal stays on → targeted therapy can be chosen from the tumor’s molecular profile.
Brake failure — squamous/SCLC emphasis: tumor-suppressor loss removes restraint. SCLC especially: TP53 + RB.
Marker / pathwayUse in this lecture
EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET, RETMajor adenocarcinoma targetable-driver framework.
KRASAdenocarcinoma; emphasized in smokers.
PD-L1Expression can identify tumors likely to benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint-directed immunotherapy in the lecture framing.
p40 vs TTF-1/napsinLineage distinction: squamous vs adenocarcinoma.

Part II — Distinctions, criteria, traps & question-stem decoding

6. Adenocarcinoma pattern recognition

PatternRecognition clueExam meaning
LepidicNormal alveolar architecture preserved; tumor cells line alveolar walls.Lecturer analogy: “butterflies on a fence.” More favorable than solid/micropapillary in the shown survival figure.
AcinarTrue gland/tubule formation.Gland-forming architecture.
PapillaryFinger-like projection with a fibrovascular core.Do not confuse with micropapillary.
MicropapillarySmall tufts/projections without fibrovascular cores.Worse-prognosis pattern emphasized by professor practice question.
SolidSheets with little obvious gland formation; mucin can establish gland lineage.More aggressive pattern in the lecture discussion.

7. Carcinoid progression & cutoffs

EntityDefining lecture rule
DIPNECHDiffuse neuroendocrine-cell hyperplasia confined to mucosa; basal lamina intact.
TumorletInvasive neuroendocrine proliferation with fibrotic stroma, ≤5 mm.
Typical carcinoidCarcinoid tumor ≥5 mm; <2 mitoses / 2 mm²; no necrosis.
Atypical carcinoid2–10 mitoses / 2 mm² and/or necrosis.
Small cellSeparate high-grade pathway; the lecturer explicitly warns that carcinoid progression does not become SCLC.
Carcinoid syndrome nuance: bronchial carcinoids are usually nonfunctional. When serotonin/histamine/bradykinin reach systemic circulation, flushing, diarrhea, edema/abdominal symptoms can occur. The transcript emphasizes that effective hepatic metabolism usually limits symptoms; liver dysfunction/metastatic burden can unmask them.

8. Mesothelioma recognition

  • Exposure: asbestos is the single major risk factor emphasized.
  • Gross: diffuse pleural thickening/encasement with invasion into lung.
  • Asbestos body: slender/dumbbell-like fiber coated by iron-rich protein → Prussian blue/iron stain.
  • Morphology: epithelioid 60%, sarcomatoid 20%, mixed 20% on the lecture slide.
  • IHC: calretinin positive, useful when epithelioid mesothelioma mimics adenocarcinoma.

9. Paraneoplastic quick table

FindingTumor / mediator
HyponatremiaSmall cell → ADH
Cushing syndromeSmall cell → ACTH
HypercalcemiaSquamous → PTH/PTHrP/PGE
HypocalcemiaSquamous → calcitonin (lecture association)
Carcinoid syndromeSerotonin / histamine / bradykinin
Lambert-EatonListed with lung-cancer paraneoplastic syndromes; classically associated with SCLC in the lecture framework.

10. What to look for in exam stems

  • Central + keratin pearls + hypercalcemia → identify squamous lineage first; then p40 / PTHrP.
  • Peripheral + glands + never-smoker → think adenocarcinoma; then ask whether EGFR/targeted therapy is the tested layer.
  • Central + small blue cells + nuclear molding + necrosis → small cell; then look for early spread, neuroendocrine markers, ADH/ACTH, TP53/RB, nonsurgical management.
  • Apical mass + ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis → Pancoast involving sympathetic chain; do not confuse with isolated recurrent-laryngeal involvement, which gives hoarseness.
  • Preserved alveoli lined by tumor cells → lepidic. Tiny tufts without a core → micropapillary.
  • NE cells confined above intact basal lamina → DIPNECH. Once invasive, use size and mitosis/necrosis to classify tumorlet vs typical vs atypical carcinoid.
  • Pleural rind/encasement + asbestos → mesothelioma; then calretinin and ferruginous bodies.

11. Common traps

Trap: “small” in small cell does not mean indolent. It is the lecture’s most aggressive major lung-cancer category.
Trap: salt-and-pepper chromatin occurs in neuroendocrine tumors broadly. Separate carcinoid from SCLC using proliferation, necrosis, mitoses, and morphology.
Trap: p40/TTF-1 are lineage markers; they are not the same concept as oncogenic driver mutations used for targeted therapy.
Trap: mesothelioma can look epithelioid and mimic adenocarcinoma. Pleural distribution + calretinin are key lecture discriminators.

Course-specific clarifications

Transcript slip: Part 1 briefly calls small cell carcinoma “the most commonest.” Elsewhere in the same lecture materials, adenocarcinoma is explicitly shown/described as the most common major lung-cancer type. This guide uses adenocarcinoma as the course-consistent classification.
Professor Practice Q1: the answer key marks “biopsy was taken with an endotracheal tube.” The pathology image itself clearly shows keratinizing squamous morphology, but that procedural inference is not supported by morphology alone. The practice engine preserves the professor key and labels the issue after submission.
Professor Practice Q5: the key marks synaptophysin, but the lecture also teaches chromogranin positivity in neuroendocrine tumors. The guide preserves the key while flagging that both are biologically consistent neuroendocrine markers.

No outside board-review material was used to replace lecture content. Where a practice item was created for this Learning Lab, it is labeled “Original” only after submission.
